promptText: When a developer runs `mvn install` on a Maven project, which of the following most accurately describes what happens, and why is it significant for interview purposes?
options: Maven runs every phase in the default lifecycle up through install (validate, compile, test, package, verify, install), and the resulting artifact is only copied into the local ~/.m2 repository — nothing is pushed to any remote repository yet.
Maven runs only the install phase itself, copying the previously built jar into the local repository without recompiling or retesting anything.
Maven runs every phase through install and also pushes the artifact to the configured remote repository, since install and deploy are functionally equivalent for a single-module project.
Maven skips the test phase by default during install, running tests only when `deploy` is invoked afterward.
explanation: Running any phase runs every prior phase in the lifecycle in order, so install implicitly triggers validate through verify first; install only writes to the local .m2 cache, and nothing leaves the machine until deploy explicitly pushes to a remote repository.

promptText: According to Maven's dependency scope rules, what happens to a dependency declared with `provided` scope, such as the Servlet API on a traditional app server?
options: It is available on the compile classpath but not the runtime classpath, and it is not passed transitively to consumers, because the container or JDK is assumed to supply it at runtime.
It is available at both compile and runtime, and it is passed transitively, making it functionally identical to the default `compile` scope except for its name.
It is available only during test execution and is excluded from both the compile and runtime classpaths of the main build.
It is never placed on any classpath and must be manually added to the runtime environment's classpath outside of Maven entirely.
explanation: provided scope is needed to compile against but must not be bundled at runtime since the runtime environment already supplies it, and unlike compile scope it does not propagate transitively to dependents.

promptText: A project depends directly on library A (which pulls in commons-io 2.11 two levels deep) and also depends directly on library B (which pulls in commons-io 2.6 one level deep, i.e. declared directly by B). Under Maven's default dependency mediation, which version of commons-io ends up on the classpath, and why?
options: commons-io 2.6, because Maven's nearest-wins mediation selects the version declared at the shallowest depth in the graph, regardless of which version is actually newer or more compatible.
commons-io 2.11, because Maven always prefers the highest version number it finds anywhere in the dependency tree.
commons-io 2.6, because Maven alphabetically sorts conflicting versions and selects the lexicographically smaller one.
The build fails immediately, because Maven refuses to resolve a graph containing two different versions of the same artifact unless dependencyManagement is used.
explanation: Nearest-wins is purely structural — it counts declaration depth, not release recency or compatibility — so a shallower but older transitive dependency can silently beat a deeper but newer one, which is why declaring the desired version explicitly at depth zero or centralizing it in a BOM is the reliable fix.

promptText: How does Gradle's default dependency conflict resolution strategy differ from Maven's, when two transitive paths pull in different versions of the same library?
options: Gradle picks the highest version found anywhere in the graph by default, while Maven picks the version declared at the shallowest depth (nearest-wins), regardless of which is actually newer.
Gradle and Maven both use nearest-wins by declaration depth, so migrating between the two tools never changes which transitive version is resolved.
Gradle requires every version conflict to be resolved manually and will always fail the build until an explicit version is pinned.
Maven picks the highest version by default, while Gradle picks whichever version is declared first in the build script regardless of depth.
explanation: Gradle's highest-wins default is generally a safer heuristic since newer is usually at least as compatible, whereas Maven's nearest-wins is purely structural and can let a shallow, older declaration silently beat a deeper, newer one — a difference that can genuinely change resolved versions when migrating between the tools.

promptText: A project already inherits from a corporate parent POM but also wants the version alignment that `spring-boot-dependencies` provides. Why must it import `spring-boot-dependencies` via `<dependencyManagement>` with `scope=import` rather than setting it as the `<parent>`?
options: Maven only allows a POM to declare a single `<parent>`, but a `<dependencyManagement>` import with scope=import can pull in version alignment from multiple BOMs at once, so importing is the only way to combine both sources.
`<parent>` and `<dependencyManagement>` import are functionally identical in Maven, so the choice is purely stylistic and has no bearing on how many BOMs can be combined.
BOMs can only be referenced through `<parent>` inheritance; `<dependencyManagement>` import is reserved exclusively for non-Spring dependencies.
Importing a BOM via `<dependencyManagement>` replaces the existing corporate parent POM entirely, removing its plugin defaults and configuration.
explanation: A parent gives inherited plugin defaults and configuration but only one is allowed per POM, while dependencyManagement imports give version alignment and can be composed from several BOMs — exactly why Spring Boot's BOM is imported rather than set as the parent when a corporate parent already exists.

promptText: Gradle marks a task `UP-TO-DATE` and skips re-executing it under what specific condition, and what happens if a custom task under-declares its inputs?
options: A task is skipped when none of its declared inputs or outputs have changed since the last successful run; if a custom task under-declares its inputs, Gradle can incorrectly skip work that should have re-run, producing a stale build.
A task is skipped whenever it previously succeeded at least once, regardless of whether any of its inputs have changed since that run.
A task is skipped only if its position in the build script's line numbering is unchanged since the previous invocation, independent of any file content changes.
Under-declaring a task's inputs causes Gradle to always rerun it unnecessarily, wasting time but never producing incorrect output.
explanation: Gradle's UP-TO-DATE check hashes declared inputs/outputs from the last run; correctly declaring them matters because under-declaring causes incorrect skips (a stale build) while over-declaring wastes caching benefit unnecessarily.

promptText: What is the precise distinction between Gradle's up-to-date checking and its build cache, and what team policy is commonly used to protect the shared cache?
options: Up-to-date checking avoids redoing work already done on the same machine over time; the build cache avoids redoing work anyone has already done anywhere, on any machine with matching inputs — and teams commonly let only CI push to the remote cache while developer machines only pull, so a bad local state can't poison it for everyone.
Up-to-date checking and the build cache are two names for the exact same mechanism, differing only in whether the `--build-cache` flag is passed on the command line.
The build cache only works within a single machine across time, while up-to-date checking is the mechanism that shares outputs across every developer and CI agent.
Both mechanisms require a remote server to function, and neither can operate using only local disk state.
explanation: Up-to-date checking is local-and-temporal (same project, same machine, over time); the build cache is content-addressed and machine-independent, which is why a CI-push/developer-pull-only policy is the standard way to keep the shared cache trustworthy.

promptText: A team notices their Gradle build is slow even when running `gradle tasks`, which does not build anything. Investigation shows a network call sitting directly at the top level of `build.gradle`, outside any task action, combined with the team's custom tasks being defined using `tasks.create(...)`. Which combination of facts explains the slowdown and the correct fix?
options: Top-level build-script code runs during the configuration phase on every single invocation regardless of which task is requested, and `tasks.create` eagerly configures a task immediately even if it is never part of the requested task graph; moving the network call into a task action and switching to `tasks.register` (lazy configuration avoidance) fixes both problems.

Top-level code only runs when the `build` task is explicitly requested, so the network call cannot be the cause; the slowdown is unrelated to `tasks.create` versus `tasks.register`, which only affects task execution order.
`tasks.create` is already lazy by default in modern Gradle, so switching to `tasks.register` would have no effect; only removing the network call would help.
The configuration phase only evaluates the root project's build script, so a network call in a subproject's build.gradle would never affect a `gradle tasks` invocation at the root.
explanation: Configuration-phase code (including a bare network call at script top level) runs on every invocation before any task executes, and eager `tasks.create` configures immediately regardless of whether the task is ever requested — both are classic causes of a build that is slow even when it does nothing, fixed by deferring work into task actions and adopting configuration avoidance via `tasks.register`.

promptText: Why does the Spring Boot Maven/Gradle plugin deliberately avoid the flattened merge approach used by the Shade and Shadow plugins, and when would you still reach for Shade/Shadow instead?
options: Spring Boot uses a nested BOOT-INF/lib jar-in-jar layout that keeps every dependency jar intact and isolated, sidestepping resource-merge collisions (like conflicting META-INF/spring.factories files) that a flattened uber-jar can hit; Shade/Shadow's flattening plus class relocation is still the right choice for a CLI tool or Lambda handler that needs a single flattened namespace.
Spring Boot's plugin and Shade/Shadow both flatten dependencies identically; the only difference is that Spring Boot's plugin is Maven-only and Shadow is Gradle-only.
Spring Boot avoids bundling dependencies altogether, requiring all libraries to be installed separately on the deployment target's classpath.
Shade and Shadow are strictly obsolete predecessors to the Spring Boot plugin and should never be used on any modern project regardless of packaging target.
explanation: The nested layout avoids the classic same-named-file-clobbering problem of naive flat fat jars, while Shade/Shadow's relocation feature is specifically valuable when you need a genuinely flattened, single-namespace artifact such as a Lambda handler.

promptText: Why does the chapter identify version ranges (e.g. declaring a dependency as `2.+` or `[1.0,2.0)`) as the biggest threat to build reproducibility?
options: A version range can silently resolve to a different, newer, previously-untested artifact on a later build of the exact same commit, without anyone changing a single line of the build file.
Version ranges cause Maven and Gradle to fail the build immediately at resolution time, so they are safe but merely inconvenient.
Version ranges only affect test-scoped dependencies and therefore cannot affect what ships in a production artifact.
Version ranges are resolved once at project creation and then cached permanently, so they behave identically to a pinned version after the first build.
explanation: Because resolution happens fresh against the range each time, the same commit can produce a different dependency graph on different days — the whole reason Gradle's dependency locking and Maven's Enforcer-banned-ranges practice exist, to force an explicit, reviewable pin instead of silent drift.

promptText: A team sets `maven.compiler.release=11` but the Maven process itself is launched under JDK 21. What guarantee does this configuration NOT provide, and what would close that gap?
options: It does not stop JDK 21's own `javac` from being the compiler that actually performs compilation — it only prevents referencing APIs newer than Java 11; only configuring a Maven Toolchain pointing at a real JDK 11 installation genuinely swaps the compiler binary used.
It fully guarantees that a real JDK 11 compiler performs the compilation, making a separate toolchains.xml configuration unnecessary in every case.
It prevents the build from running at all unless JDK 11 is the JDK that launched the `mvn` command.
It only affects runtime behavior of the packaged jar and has no effect on which APIs can be referenced at compile time.
explanation: `maven.compiler.release` constrains the API surface allowed but the actual `javac` invoked is still whichever JDK launched Maven; a genuine toolchain declaration in toolchains.xml is the only mechanism that swaps the actual compiler binary to match the declared version.

promptText: A team marks a custom `GenerateApiDocs` task as `@CacheableTask`, but the task's action embeds the current wall-clock timestamp into its generated output file. What specific failure mode does this risk, and why is `compileJava` safe to cache by contrast?
options: This risks cache poisoning: since the cache key is based on declared inputs, a build with matching inputs but a different actual run time would incorrectly reuse a stale cached output containing an old timestamp; `compileJava` is safely cacheable because its output is fully deterministic given the same source and classpath, with no non-deterministic embedded state.
This is safe because Gradle automatically detects any embedded timestamp in a task's output and excludes cacheable tasks from ever using stale results.
The risk only affects up-to-date checking, not the build cache, since the build cache always re-executes non-deterministic tasks regardless of the `@CacheableTask` annotation.
`compileJava` is not actually cacheable by default in Gradle, so this scenario has no valid safe-cache comparison to draw.
explanation: A cache key is computed only from declared inputs/outputs and the implementation class, so a task with genuinely non-deterministic behavior (like an embedded timestamp) can silently serve a wrong cached result to every future build with matching inputs — exactly the cache poisoning failure mode that must never be marked cacheable.

promptText: In a Maven multi-module reactor build with modules listed as `<module>api</module>`, `<module>common</module>`, `<module>service</module>`, where `api` depends on `service` and `service` depends on `common`, what determines the actual build order?
options: The reactor computes build order from the inter-module dependency graph (common, then service, then api), completely independent of the order modules are listed under `<modules>` in the parent POM.
Modules always build in exactly the order listed in the parent POM's `<modules>` block, so here the order would be api, common, service regardless of dependencies.
Modules build in alphabetical order by artifactId unless `-pl` is explicitly passed on the command line.
Maven builds all modules simultaneously in parallel by default with no ordering guarantees, since ordering is only relevant when `-T` is passed.
explanation: The reactor reads every module's POM first, builds a dependency graph between them, and derives a build order that respects it — a detail worth knowing since many candidates wrongly assume listing order controls build order.

promptText: What is the key lifecycle-binding difference between Maven's Surefire and Failsafe plugins?
options: Surefire runs `*Test.java` unit tests bound to the `test` phase and fails the build immediately before packaging, while Failsafe runs `*IT.java` integration tests bound to `integration-test`/`verify`, evaluating failures only at `verify` so a broken integration test does not block artifact creation.
Surefire and Failsafe both run at the exact same phase and only differ in which test naming convention they scan for, with no difference in when failures actually block the build.
Failsafe replaces Surefire entirely in modern Maven projects, so any project using Failsafe should remove Surefire from its build.
Surefire runs after packaging to test the assembled artifact, while Failsafe runs before compilation to validate test source syntax.
explanation: The phase binding is deliberate: unit tests must gate packaging immediately, while integration tests need a real packaged artifact to exercise and should not block artifact creation the way a broken unit test does.

promptText: A team configures its Gradle remote build cache so that only CI can push (`isPush = System.getenv("CI") != null`) while developer machines only pull. A developer argues this policy alone is sufficient to guarantee the shared cache is always trustworthy. What is the flaw in that reasoning?
options: The CI-only push policy only protects against a compromised or misconfigured developer machine polluting the shared cache; it does nothing to prevent CI itself from pushing a bad entry if a task is incorrectly marked `@CacheableTask` with non-deterministic behavior (e.g. an embedded timestamp), since CI's own poisoned output would still be pushed and trusted by everyone.
The policy is fully sufficient on its own, since CI is defined as inherently deterministic and therefore incapable of producing a poisoned cache entry.
CI-only push actually prevents any caching from occurring at all, since developer machines can never populate the cache under this configuration.
This policy has nothing to do with cache correctness; it exists purely to reduce network bandwidth costs on developer machines.
explanation: The push/pull trust boundary defends against one specific risk (an untrusted developer machine corrupting the shared cache) but is orthogonal to the separate discipline of correctly declaring task inputs/outputs and avoiding `@CacheableTask` on non-deterministic tasks — both safeguards are needed together, since CI itself can push a poisoned entry if a task is mis-declared as cacheable.
